warmup.q: Inside coroutineScope { }, you start val risk = async { riskScore(id) } and then do 500 ms of other work before calling risk.await(). The risk call throws at 100 ms. When does anything happen?
options: Only at await(), at 500 ms: until then the exception waits inside the Deferred
At 100 ms: the scope is cancelled, the other work stops, and coroutineScope throws
Never: an exception in async is ignored unless someone awaits it
At 100 ms the exception is printed by the uncaught handler, and await() returns null
warmup.why: A failed child cancels its parent at once, and that is as true for async as for launch. The exception waits in the Deferred only when the parent is a supervisor or there is no parent. Here the scope is cancelled at 100 ms and await() is never reached.

sections.h: launch and async both report a failure to their parent at once
sections.html:
A coroutine that ends with an exception other than CancellationException has failed, and a failed child tells its parent at once. With a regular job, the parent then does what lesson 3 of this track described: it cancels its other children, waits for them to stop, and fails with the same exception. That holds for launch and for async alike.

The async half surprises people. Many expect a failure in async to wait in the Deferred until somebody calls await, the way a failed CompletableFuture waits for join. It doesn't:

Java
// Java equivalent: a failed future tells nobody until someone joins it
CompletableFuture<Score> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> riskScore(paymentId), pool);
CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> postToLedger(paymentId), pool);
Thread.sleep(500);                                  // passed: the ledger task keeps running too
risk.join();                                        // the failure shows up only here
Kotlin
coroutineScope {
    val risk = async { riskScore(paymentId) }      // throws at 100 ms
    launch { postToLedger(paymentId) }
    delay(500)                                     // never passed: the scope is cancelled at 100 ms
    risk.await()
}

At 100 ms the risk call fails, the scope cancels the ledger call, and coroutineScope throws the risk exception to its caller. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc says it directly: async follows the same rules, and only when the parent is a supervisor or there is no parent is the exception "only available through the returned Deferred".

So a try around await does not protect the scope. By the time await would throw, the child has already cancelled the scope. runCatching { risk.await() } inside coroutineScope is a common bug, and it is one of the bugs in this lesson's lab.

Where do launch and async differ, then? Only when a failure has nobody above it to tell. A launch at the root hands its exception to a handler, which the next section covers. An async at the root keeps it in the Deferred, and await rethrows it. That is the same split as execute and submit on a Java executor: execute sends a task's exception to the thread's uncaught exception handler, while submit keeps it in the Future for get.

try.title: Fail an async that nobody awaits
steps: Read AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt. The risk call fails at 100 ms, and the body only awaits it at 500 ms. Predict which lines print, and when.
Run it.
Run it with -Pargs=supervisor, which uses supervisorScope. Predict first: when does the failure surface now, and what happens to the ledger child?
Run the Java twin.

code.title: AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope import java.io.IOException private var t0 = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { t0 = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" try { val body: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { val risk = async { delay(100); throw IOException("risk service down") } // nobody awaits this yet launch { try { delay(1_000); log("ledger: done") } finally { log("ledger: finally") } } delay(500) log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to await risk") risk.await() } if (supervised) supervisorScope(body) else coroutineScope(body) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: IOException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt: a failed CompletableFuture tells nobody. // The failure sits in the future until someone joins it, and the sibling task runs on. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava { static long T0; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { T0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture<Void> risk = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("risk service down")); // nobody joins this yet }, pool); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { try { sleep(1_000); log("ledger: done"); } finally { log("ledger: finally"); } }, pool); sleep(500); log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to join risk"); try { risk.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { log("caller caught: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); } } // close() waits for the ledger task, which nobody cancelled log("pool closed"); } }

try.expect: Plain: at about 100 ms, ledger: finally and caller caught: risk service down. The body's 500 ms line never prints. With -Pargs=supervisor, the failed async does nothing on its own. The body prints at 500 ms, await rethrows, and because the block itself threw, supervisorScope cancels the ledger child (ledger: finally) and rethrows. The Java twin is the contrast: nothing reacts at 100 ms, the caller sees the failure only when it joins at 500 ms, and the ledger task runs on to 1,000 ms.

sections.h: CoroutineExceptionHandler is a last resort, and only roots use it
sections.html:
CoroutineExceptionHandler is a context element that receives the exceptions nobody else handled. It is for logging and metrics. By the time it runs the coroutine has already finished, so there is nothing left to recover.

The rule that trips people up: only root coroutines use it. A child passes its exception to its parent, all the way up to the root, so a handler installed on a child is never called. A handler takes effect in two places. One is a coroutine launched straight into a scope whose job is not a coroutine, such as CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + handler).launch { }. The other is a direct child of a supervisor, which handles its own failure the way a root does (next section). It never takes effect on async, because an async keeps its exception for await.

Java
// Java equivalent: the thread's uncaught handler sees execute() failures, never submit() ones
Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> log.warn("task failed on {}", t.getName(), e);
ExecutorService webhooks = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, r -> {
    Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks");
    t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler);
    return t;
});
webhooks.execute(() -> { throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("webhook 503")); });   // handler gets it
Kotlin
coroutineScope {
    launch(handler) { throw IOException("webhook 503") }   // ignored: this is a child
}                                                          // coroutineScope throws IOException

val webhooks = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler)
webhooks.launch { throw IOException("webhook 503") }        // a root: the handler gets it

If there is no handler in the context, the library falls back to the JVM's last-resort path: handlers registered through ServiceLoader, then the thread's uncaught exception handler, which usually prints a stack trace to stderr. In a service that is one log line and nothing more.

When several children fail at once, the first exception wins and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. Read the suppressed list before you decide only one call failed. Handlers ignore CancellationException, since a cancel is not a failure.

The practical upshot: install one handler on each long-lived scope you own, at the line where you create the scope, and use it to log and count. Don't sprinkle handlers on launch calls inside request code. There, a failure should reach the request, where an ordinary try around coroutineScope deals with it.

try.title: Find out where a handler runs
steps: Read HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt. It installs the same handler in three places. Predict which of the three prints handler got.
Run it.
In case 1, swap coroutineScope for supervisorScope and run it again. Predict first.

code.title: HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException fun main() = runBlocking { val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> println(" handler got: ${e.message} (from ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name})") } println("1. handler on a child inside coroutineScope:") try { coroutineScope { launch(handler + CoroutineName("child")) { throw IOException("webhook 503") } } } catch (e: IOException) { println(" coroutineScope threw: ${e.message} (the child's handler was ignored)") } println("2. handler on a scope with a SupervisorJob, root launch:") val webhooks = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler) webhooks.launch(CoroutineName("root-launch")) { throw IOException("webhook 503") }.join() println("3. the same scope, root async that nobody awaits:") val d = webhooks.async(CoroutineName("root-async")) { throw IOException("webhook 503") } delay(100) println(" nothing printed: the failure waits in the Deferred") try { d.await() } catch (e: IOException) { println(" await threw: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: HandlerOnlyAtRootJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt: execute() sends a task's exception to the thread's // uncaught exception handler (like a root launch and its handler), while submit() keeps it // inside the Future until someone calls get() (like a root async and await). package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class HandlerOnlyAtRootJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler got: " + e.getCause().getMessage() + " (on " + t.getName() + ")"); ExecutorService webhooks = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler); return t; }); Runnable failing = () -> { throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("webhook 503")); }; System.out.println("1. execute(): the exception reaches the thread's handler"); webhooks.execute(failing); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println("2. submit() that nobody waits for:"); Future<?> f = webhooks.submit(failing); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(" nothing printed: the failure waits in the Future"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" get threw: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); } webhooks.shutdown(); webhooks.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: Only case 2 prints handler got: webhook 503 (from root-launch). In case 1 the handler on the child is ignored and coroutineScope throws. In case 3 nothing prints until await rethrows. After your change, case 1 prints handler got too: a direct child of supervisorScope handles its own failure like a root, and the scope returns normally. The Java twin shows the same split: execute reaches the thread's handler, submit waits in the Future until get.

sections.h: A supervisor lets children fail alone
sections.html:
Sometimes siblings shouldn't care about each other. The payment is captured, and now an email, an SMS and a push notification go out. An outage at the SMS gateway must not cancel the email. That is the job of a supervisor: a job whose children can fail independently. A child's failure doesn't cancel its siblings or the supervisor. Cancellation still flows down, so cancelling the supervisor cancels every child.

There are two ways to get one. supervisorScope { } is the supervisor version of coroutineScope, for work the caller waits for:

Java
// Java equivalent: futures are independent, so each one handles its own failure
Map<Channel, CompletableFuture<Outcome>> sends = new EnumMap<>(Channel.class);
senders.forEach((ch, s) -> sends.put(ch, CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> s.send(paymentId), pool)
    .handle((ok, e) -> e == null ? new Delivered() : new Failed(e.getMessage()))));
CompletableFuture.allOf(sends.values().toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
Kotlin
suspend fun notifyAll(paymentId: String): Map<Channel, Outcome> = supervisorScope {
    val sends = senders.mapValues { (_, s) -> async { s.send(paymentId) } }
    sends.mapValues { (_, d) ->
        try { d.await(); Outcome.Delivered }
        catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
        catch (e: Exception) { Outcome.Failed(e.message ?: e.toString()) }
    }
}

With async children, each failure stays in its Deferred, and await rethrows it where you can catch it. With launch children there is no await, so the failure goes to the handler in the context. supervisorScope doesn't install one, so without your own handler it lands in the uncaught exception handler.

SupervisorJob() is the supervisor for a scope you own (lesson 3 of this track): CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler). Every launch into that scope is a child that can fail alone, and its failure goes to the scope's handler. The library's own MainScope() is built the same way, from a SupervisorJob and the main dispatcher.

One rule doesn't change. If the body of supervisorScope throws, the whole scope is cancelled, children included. Supervision covers the children, not the block itself, which is why the Try it in the first section cancelled the ledger child when await rethrew.

Pick per call, not per service. A payment details endpoint that needs all three of its calls wants coroutineScope, so one failure cancels the rest at once. Notifications, cache warm-ups and optional enrichments want a supervisor.

code.title: SupervisorDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope import java.io.IOException private var started = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg)) // supervisorScope installs no handler of its own, so failed launch children need one in the context private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log("handler: ${e.message}") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking(handler) { started = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" val sendAll: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { launch { try { delay(300); log("email sent") } finally { log("email: finally") } } launch { delay(50); throw IOException("sms gateway down") } launch { try { delay(100); log("push sent") } finally { log("push: finally") } } } try { if (supervised) supervisorScope(sendAll) else coroutineScope(sendAll) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: IOException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: SupervisorDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SupervisorDemo.kt: CompletableFutures are independent by default, like // children of a supervisor. Nothing cancels the siblings, so each future handles its own failure. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class SupervisorDemoJava { static long started; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { started = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture<Void> email = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(300); log("email sent"); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> sms = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(50); throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("sms gateway down")); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> push = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); log("push sent"); }, pool); // each failure is handled where it happens; the siblings never hear about it CompletableFuture<Void> smsHandled = sms.exceptionally(e -> { log("handled: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); return null; }); CompletableFuture.allOf(email, smsHandled, push).join(); log("all three settled"); } } }

try.expect: With coroutineScope, email and push are cancelled at about 50 ms (their finally lines) and the caller catches sms gateway down. With -Pargs=supervisor, the handler prints at about 50 ms, push is sent at about 100 ms, email at about 300 ms, and the scope returns normally. The Java twin behaves like the supervisor without being asked: futures are independent, so each one has to handle its own failure.

sections.html:
Here is the most common wrong fix. A merchant webhook in a capture handler keeps cancelling its siblings when the merchant's server is down, so someone writes:

Java
// Java equivalent: hand the task to some other, longer-lived executor
try (var request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> webhooks.post(event));     // no longer part of this request
    request.submit(() -> ledger.record(event));
}
Kotlin
coroutineScope {
    launch(SupervisorJob()) { webhooks.post(event) }   // meant as "make this child supervised"
    launch { ledger.record(event) }
}

It reads like "a supervised child". It is something else. A Job in a builder's context replaces the parent, so the new coroutine becomes the child of that fresh SupervisorJob, which has no parent of its own. The coroutine has left the tree. coroutineScope doesn't wait for it, cancelling the request doesn't cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler or the uncaught exception handler instead of to the request. It is GlobalScope from lesson 3 of this track, spelled differently.

The builder docs say it plainly: passing a Job there breaks structured concurrency, and it doesn't throw "only for backward compatibility reasons". kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 goes further and deprecates the overload, so the compiler now warns: "Passing a Job to coroutine builders breaks structured concurrency, leading to hard-to-diagnose errors." The same rule applies to async and withContext. The one documented exception is withContext(NonCancellable) for cleanup, from lesson 5 of this track.

Put the supervisor where it belongs. Inside a function, wrap the children in supervisorScope { }. For background work, give the owning class a scope built with SupervisorJob() in its constructor, and launch into that scope. Then the work is supervised and still owned: the scope waits for it, counts it and cancels it on shutdown.

When you see launch(SupervisorJob()), launch(Job()) or async(SupervisorJob()) in a review, ask what the author wanted. Usually the answer is one of those two shapes.

try.title: Cancel a request and watch the trap child survive
steps: Read SupervisorTrap.kt. The request is cancelled at 100 ms. Predict which of the two children prints after that.
Run it. Look for the deprecation warning in the Gradle output when the demo compiles.
Delete SupervisorJob() from the first launch and run it again.
Run the Java twin, where the detached task lives on a shared executor.

code.title: SupervisorTrap.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var since = 0L private fun stamp(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main() = runBlocking { since = System.nanoTime() val request = launch { // looks like "a supervised child". It is a child of a brand-new SupervisorJob instead, // so it has left the request's tree: nobody waits for it and nobody cancels it. launch(SupervisorJob()) { delay(300) stamp("trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me") } launch { try { delay(300); stamp("normal child: done") } finally { stamp("normal child: finally") } } } delay(100) request.cancelAndJoin() stamp("request cancelled and joined") delay(400) stamp("main done") }

alt.title: SupervisorTrapJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SupervisorTrap.kt: a task sent to some other executor is not part of the // request. Shutting the request's executor down interrupts its own tasks, not that one. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SupervisorTrapJava { static long since; static void stamp(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { since = System.nanoTime(); ExecutorService shared = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // what launch(SupervisorJob()) amounts to ExecutorService request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); shared.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("detached task: still running, nobody cancelled me"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("detached task: interrupted"); } }); request.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("request task: done"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("request task: interrupted"); } }); Thread.sleep(100); request.shutdownNow(); request.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); stamp("request cancelled and joined"); Thread.sleep(400); shared.shutdown(); stamp("main done"); } }

try.expect: The normal child's finally runs at about 100 ms and the request is cancelled and joined. Then, at about 300 ms, trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me prints: it was never part of the request's tree. After your change, neither child prints after the cancel. The Java twin shows the same leak with a task on a shared pool. (The warning appears only on the first compile; once the class is compiled, Gradle doesn't print it again.)

analogy: Think of a coroutine family as a film crew on location. With a regular job, the crew is one unit: if the camera operator is injured, the director stops the shoot, sends everyone home and reports the incident to the studio. A supervisor is a courier depot instead. If one courier's van breaks down, the depot logs it and the other couriers finish their rounds, but when the depot closes for the night, everyone comes back. The exception handler is the depot's incident book: it records what went wrong after the fact and fixes nothing. launch(SupervisorJob()) is hiring a freelancer through a different agency. They do the work, but your depot doesn't know they exist and won't call them back at closing time. The analogy breaks at the start of the trip: a real crew member can see the director wave. A coroutine only hears about a cancel at its next suspension point.
world: After a capture succeeds, a payments service usually fires several side effects: merchant webhooks, customer notifications, loyalty points, an analytics event. None of them should cancel the others, and none should fail the capture. If the request waits for them, wrap them in supervisorScope and turn each await into an outcome. If they run after the response, give a component one scope built with SupervisorJob(), Dispatchers.IO and a handler that logs with the payment id and increments a failure metric, and close it in @PreDestroy. The Kafka partition worker from lesson 3 of this track wants the same swap: with a SupervisorJob, one bad record no longer cancels every batch in the partition. And keep anything that must not be lost, such as the ledger write, out of fire-and-forget code entirely. It belongs in the request's own scope, or in an outbox table that a worker drains.
mistake: The most common mistake is trying to contain a failure at the wrong place: wrapping await() in try or runCatching inside coroutineScope, or putting a CoroutineExceptionHandler on a child launch. Both look like error handling, and neither runs before the damage is done, because a failed child cancels its parent the moment it fails. The scope and its other children are already cancelled when your catch would run, and the handler on a child is never consulted. Decide first whether the siblings should share a fate. If they should, let the failure propagate and catch it around the whole coroutineScope. If they shouldn't, use supervisorScope (or a scope with a SupervisorJob), and then a try around each await or a handler on the scope does work.

compare.title: A background sender: pool with an uncaught handler vs supervisor scope with a handler

java.title: WebhookSender.java
java.html: class WebhookSender implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); // last resort for task failures, like a CoroutineExceptionHandler t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("webhook failed", e)); return t; }); void post(Event event) { pool.execute(() -> client.post(event)); // execute, not submit: failures reach the handler } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } }

kotlin.title: WebhookSender.kt
kotlin.html: class WebhookSender(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("webhook failed", e) } // SupervisorJob: one failed post doesn't cancel the others or the scope private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun post(event: Event): Job = scope.launch { client.post(event) } // a root child: failures reach the handler fun close() = scope.cancel() }

compare.note: The two defaults are opposite. A Java thread pool is a supervisor without being asked: tasks never cancel each other, so you only have to make sure failures are seen (execute sends them to the uncaught handler, submit hides them in a Future nobody reads). A coroutine scope with a plain Job fails together, which is right for a request and wrong for a background sender, so you opt in with SupervisorJob(). After that the shapes match: launch is execute and goes to the handler, async is submit and keeps its failure for await. What Kotlin adds is the tree. The scope still knows every child, so close() cancels the sends in flight, and code that calls post from a test can wait for them.

steps.say: A capture handler posts a merchant webhook. The merchant's server was down, the webhook failure cancelled the ledger write, and someone fixed it like this. Tests became flaky (webhooks fire after the test has ended) and shutdown logs show webhooks posting into a closed HTTP client. Why?
steps.code: suspend fun capture(cmd: Capture) = coroutineScope { val result = issuer.capture(cmd) launch { ledger.record(result) } launch(SupervisorJob()) { webhooks.post(result.toEvent()) } // the "fix" result }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same fix: the webhook goes to a shared pool nobody owns CaptureResult capture(Capture cmd) throws Exception { CaptureResult result = issuer.capture(cmd); try (var request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { request.submit(() -> ledger.record(result)); SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> webhooks.post(result.toEvent())); // the "fix" } return result; }

steps.say: The SupervisorJob() became the webhook's parent, so the webhook left the request's tree. Nothing waits for it and nothing cancels it. Decide what the author wanted. The response shouldn't wait for the merchant, so the webhook belongs to a long-lived owner. Give that owner a supervisor scope and a handler.
steps.code: class WebhookDispatcher(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) : AutoCloseable { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> log.warn("webhook ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name} failed", e) // 1. log with the payment id } // 2. supervised and owned: children fail alone, close() still reaches them private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun post(event: Event): Job = scope.launch(CoroutineName(event.paymentId)) { webhooks.post(event) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the dispatcher owns its pool and its failure handler class WebhookDispatcher implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("webhook failed", e)); // 1. log return t; }); // 2. owned: close() reaches every task void post(Event event) { pool.execute(() -> webhooks.post(event)); } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } }

steps.say: The capture goes back to a plain structured scope. The ledger write must succeed or fail with the capture, so it stays a child. The webhook is handed to its owner.
steps.code: suspend fun capture(cmd: Capture): CaptureResult { val result = issuer.capture(cmd) ledger.record(result) // 3. part of the request: a failure fails the capture webhookDispatcher.post(result.toEvent()) // handed off: the owner deals with failures return result }

alt.html: CaptureResult capture(Capture cmd) { CaptureResult result = issuer.capture(cmd); ledger.record(result); // 3. part of the request webhookDispatcher.post(result.toEvent()); // handed off to its owner return result; }

steps.say: If the response must include whether the webhook got through, the request does wait, and the right shape is supervisorScope with an outcome per call instead.
steps.code: suspend fun captureAndNotify(cmd: Capture): Pair<CaptureResult, Boolean> = supervisorScope { val result = issuer.capture(cmd) ledger.record(result) // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone val hook = async { webhooks.post(result.toEvent()) } val delivered = try { hook.await(); true } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { false } result to delivered }

alt.html: Map.Entry<CaptureResult, Boolean> captureAndNotify(Capture cmd) { CaptureResult result = issuer.capture(cmd); ledger.record(result); // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone boolean delivered = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> webhooks.post(result.toEvent()), pool) .handle((ok, e) -> e == null) .join(); return Map.entry(result, delivered); }

steps.say: Self-check: in step 4, the ledger write throws. What happens to the webhook call? (Nothing yet: it hasn't started. The exception is thrown from the supervisorScope block itself, so the scope is cancelled and rethrows. A supervisor protects siblings from each other, not from a failing block.)

lab.title: Notifications that fail one channel at a time
steps: Run the tests. Five of eight fail. Notifications.kt holds the shared model: Channel, Sender and Outcome.
In NotifyAll.kt, switch coroutineScope to supervisorScope, so a failed send stays in its own Deferred.
Give each send its own deadline with withTimeoutOrNull(timeout) inside the async, and map a null result to Outcome.Failed("timed out").
Replace runCatching around await() with a try that rethrows CancellationException and turns any other exception into Outcome.Failed(message). The notifyAll tests should now pass.
In NotificationService.kt, build the scope from dispatcher + SupervisorJob() + handler, where the handler calls reportFailure with the payment id from the coroutine's CoroutineName.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then try launch(SupervisorJob() + ...) in notifyLater and see which tests catch it.
hints: withTimeoutOrNull(timeout) { sender.send(paymentId) } returns Unit when the send finishes and null when it times out.
CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, error -> ... } gets the failed coroutine's context, so context[CoroutineName]?.name is the payment id that notifyLater set.
A handler is used only by root coroutines. Children launched straight into a scope built with SupervisorJob() count as roots, so a handler in the scope's context sees their failures.
The close and pending tests already pass on the stub. They are there to catch the launch(SupervisorJob()) trap.

drill.title: A supervised background worker from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class LoyaltyUpdater(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) with fun award(paymentId: String): Job that calls a suspending points.add(paymentId) in the background. One failed award must not stop the others; every failure is logged with log.warn; and suspend fun close() cancels pending awards and waits for them.

answer.html: class LoyaltyUpdater(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("loyalty award failed", e) } private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun award(paymentId: String): Job = scope.launch { points.add(paymentId) } suspend fun close() { scope.coroutineContext.job.cancelAndJoin() } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a pool is independent by default; route failures to a handler class LoyaltyUpdater implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "loyalty"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("loyalty award failed", e)); return t; }); void award(String paymentId) { pool.execute(() -> points.add(paymentId)); } @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdownNow(); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

recap: A failed child cancels its parent at once, whether it was started with launch or async, and whether or not anyone awaits it.
launch and async differ only at the root: a root launch goes to a CoroutineExceptionHandler, a root async keeps the exception for await.
CoroutineExceptionHandler runs only for root coroutines and direct children of a supervisor, never for async. It is for logging, not recovery.
A supervisor lets children fail alone, while cancellation still flows down. Use supervisorScope inside a function and SupervisorJob() in the constructor of a scope you own.
launch(SupervisorJob()) replaces the parent and detaches the child from the tree. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates passing a Job to builders.
When several children fail, the first exception wins and the rest are attached as suppressed.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why their runCatching { quote.await() } inside coroutineScope didn't stop one failed FX quote from failing the whole pricing call, and why moving a CoroutineExceptionHandler onto the async didn't help either. Explain, and say what you would write instead.
explain.answer: In a regular coroutineScope, a child that fails reports to its parent straight away, whether it's a launch or an async and whether or not anyone has awaited it. So the moment the quote failed, the scope was cancelled, the other quotes were cancelled, and coroutineScope rethrew the exception. The runCatching around await came too late to matter. The handler did nothing because handlers only run for root coroutines, and an async never uses one anyway: it keeps its exception for await. If one failed quote should not sink the others, use supervisorScope. There, a failed async child just stores its exception in its Deferred, so a try around each await, rethrowing CancellationException, turns each quote into a value or a failure. If the call really needs all the quotes, keep coroutineScope and catch the exception around the whole scope instead.

deeper.html:
SupervisorJob(parent) takes an optional parent, and that link works in one direction. If the parent is cancelled or fails, the supervisor is cancelled with it. A failure of one of the supervisor's children doesn't travel up. That makes CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob(appJob) + dispatcher) a good shape for a component scope that should die with the application but never take it down.

supervisorScope and SupervisorJob differ in one detail that bites in tests. supervisorScope waits for all its children, like coroutineScope, and rethrows if its own block throws. A scope built with SupervisorJob() never "completes" on its own: it is a long-lived container, and you end it with cancel(). That is why the lab's NotificationService has an explicit close().

The last-resort path on the JVM is pluggable. kotlinx.coroutines looks up CoroutineExceptionHandler implementations through ServiceLoader and calls each of them before the thread's uncaught exception handler. kotlinx-coroutines-test uses that hook to collect exceptions from coroutines that escape the test, and since 1.7 runTest fails at the end if any were collected, even from coroutines that are not children of the test. That is why the lab's stub fails loudly instead of printing a stack trace and passing.

Finally, CancellationException again. Since a cancel is not a failure, it never goes to a handler, and a child that ends with it never cancels its parent. That is the rule that made the runCatching loop in lesson 5 of this track so dangerous, and it is also why withTimeout inside a launch fails quietly. Code that turns a timeout into a real error (withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out")) produces an IllegalStateException, which does travel up the tree.
